summary_html: Agency **files a court petition** to open a **dependency** (or similar) case. Federal funding frameworks (IV-E/ASFA) link court oversight, reasonable-efforts findings, and permanency timelines to downstream actions.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — court findings; timelines; permanency planning  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal review of court/agency performance measures

primary_citations.citation_text: California - Penal Code §§ 11164–11174.3 (CANRA – Child Abuse and Neglect Reporting Act)
California - Welfare & Institutions Code § 300 et seq. (Juvenile dependency proceedings)

regulations_applicable.title: Title 22 - Social Security (DSS Child Welfare Regulations)
Title 11 - Law (DOJ Child Abuse Central Index)

provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court held that California's dependency scheme satisfies due process even though the detriment findings at review hearings that make a section 366.26 termination hearing possible are made by a preponderance of the evidence, because removal must first be proved by clear and convincing evidence and unfitness is established cumulatively before termination.
key_cases.relevance: Describes the sequence from petition through jurisdiction, disposition and review that a filed dependency petition sets in motion, and the burden the agency bears at each step.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the standard of proof for termination of parental rights under the child dependency statutes comports with the requirements of due process.

key_cases.holding: The court held that the first clause of Welfare and Institutions Code section 300(b)(1) authorizes dependency jurisdiction on a parent's failure or inability to adequately supervise or protect the child without any separate finding that the parent was neglectful, blameworthy or unfit.
key_cases.relevance: Governs whether the facts alleged in a petition state a basis for dependency jurisdiction under section 300(b)(1).
key_cases.quote: As we explain, this history makes clear that the Legislature did not intend to impose a parental fault requirement in the first clause of section 300(b)(1).

key_cases.holding: The court held that because the juvenile court has a continuing duty to inquire into a child's Indian status, a parent may challenge an ICWA-inapplicability finding on appeal from a later termination order even though no timely appeal was taken from the earlier order that subsumed the finding.
key_cases.relevance: Requires the court to address Indian status when the petition is filed and at every hearing thereafter.
key_cases.quote: In sum, a juvenile court has an affirmative and continuing duty in all dependency proceedings to inquire into a child's Indian status.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the Court of Appeal and held that a father's prolonged and egregious sexual abuse of his daughter can be substantial evidence supporting dependency jurisdiction over his sons under section 300(j), even though the sons were never abused and were unaware of their sister's abuse.
key_cases.relevance: Governs the sufficiency of section 300(j) sibling-risk allegations in a dependency petition and the substantial-evidence review the jurisdictional finding receives.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that a father's prolonged and egregious sexual abuse of his own child may provide substantial evidence to support a finding that all his children are juvenile court dependents.

key_cases.holding: The court reversed the Court of Appeal and held that 'substance abuse' under section 300(b)(1)(D) bears its ordinary meaning and needs no medical diagnosis or DSM showing, but rejected the 'tender years' presumption that a substance abuse finding is prima facie evidence of an inability to provide regular care and of a substantial risk of serious physical harm.
key_cases.relevance: Requires an agency filing a section 300(b)(1) petition to plead and prove inability to provide regular care and a substantial risk of serious physical harm, not merely substance abuse.
key_cases.quote: Substance abuse, when shown to exist, should not be regarded as automatically amounting to prima facie evidence of the other facts required for dependency jurisdiction.

key_cases.holding: The court held that dependency jurisdiction under section 300(f), which applies where a parent caused another child's death through neglect, may rest on a breach of ordinary care and does not require criminal negligence.
key_cases.relevance: Supplies the California Supreme Court's construction of the section 300(f) ground for filing a petition as to surviving children after a sibling's death.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that section 300(f) does not limit its application to criminal negligence.
